idiom_name: module privacy plus zero-sized capability tokens (private fields, sealed traits)
implementation_notes: Rust is the one language here where the pattern's structural requirement is enforced by the compiler: everything is private by default, pub(crate) and pub(in path) scope visibility to a tree, and a type whose fields are private cannot be constructed or mutated from outside its module at all - the attempt is a compile error, not a warning, so a resource held behind a mediating method is genuinely unreachable to safe code. The capability element is expressible in the type system too: a zero-sized token whose field is private cannot be forged outside the monitor, so a method that takes Capability<Read> by value can only be called with proof that the monitor granted the access, and sealed traits keep downstream crates from implementing the policy interface. What stays outside the guarantee is unsafe code inside the crate - transmute, raw pointers, FFI - and the crate boundary itself: pub(crate) is crate-wide, so a sibling module can bypass the monitor unless the monitor lives in its own crate.
pitfalls: pub(crate) is not privacy against the rest of the crate: any module in the same crate can reach crate-visible items, so the trust boundary is the crate - put the monitor in its own crate when the same crate also contains the code under mediation.

Deriving Clone, Copy, Default or Deserialize on the resource or the capability creates construction paths the monitor never approved; derive on the mediator's terms only, and never on the capability type.
Leaking a reference to internal state (&mut, Deref, AsRef or a getter returning &Store) lets safe code bypass every later check; hand out owned values or guards that re-check.

unsafe, transmute, FFI and build scripts can forge capabilities or alias the resource, and a dependency's unsafe code sits inside your trust boundary too - fence unsafe out of the monitor's dependency closure.
